title: Scampi
subtitle: Breaded langoustines or king prawns, deep-fried until golden
excerpt: Whole langoustine tails or large prawns in a crisp, golden breadcrumb coating, fried until the outside is crunchy and the shellfish inside is just cooked. Served with tartare sauce and lemon.
sourceNotes: Scampi in breadcrumbs became a fixture on British pub and restaurant menus from the 1960s onwards, marketed initially from Scottish and Norwegian langoustines. By the 1970s it was one of the most ordered pub-food items in the country. Recipe developed from first principles.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Bread the scampi up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerate before frying.

content.text: Scampi is breaded shellfish, fried until the coating is deeply golden and the langoustine or prawn inside is just cooked. The breading follows the same three-stage method as chicken goujons: flour, egg, then breadcrumbs. The key difference is oil temperature: langoustines cook faster than chicken, so the oil must be hot enough (180 degrees C) to colour the crust before the delicate shellfish overcooks.

items.prepNote: large, peeled and deveined, or raw langoustine tails
for deep or shallow frying, enough to fill the pan 5 cm deep

content.text: Pat {{prawns-raw}} of prawns or langoustine tails completely dry with kitchen paper.

Set up three bowls: one with {{plain-flour}} of seasoned flour, one with {{eggs}} beaten eggs, one with {{breadcrumbs-dried}} of breadcrumbs. Pass each piece through flour (shake off excess), egg, then breadcrumbs (press to coat). Refrigerate for 30 minutes.
Heat {{sunflower-oil}} of oil in a large, deep pan over medium-high heat to 180 degrees C. Test with a breadcrumb: it should sizzle and colour within 30 seconds.
Fry in batches of 6 to 8, without overcrowding. Cook for 2 to 3 minutes, turning once, until deep golden. Drain on kitchen paper and season with salt immediately.
Serve immediately with lemon wedges and tartare sauce.

rows.symptom: Coating falls off in the oil
rows.cause: Shellfish wet when breaded, or flour stage skipped
rows.fix: Pat completely dry before breading. All three stages are necessary: flour creates a surface for the egg to grip.

rows.cause: Oil not hot enough so shellfish cooked too long in tepid oil
rows.fix: The oil must be at 180 degrees C. Test with a breadcrumb first. At the right temperature, scampi needs only 2 to 3 minutes.
Cold oil soaks into the coating instead of sealing it. Use a thermometer or the breadcrumb test and do not rush.

rows.symptom: Shellfish is still raw inside when coating is golden
rows.cause: Oil too hot, coating too thick
rows.fix: Lower the oil temperature slightly. Use a thinner coating: one even layer of crumbs, not a thick shell.

content.text: Scampi in a basket became one of the defining dishes of British pub food in the 1960s and 1970s. It was sold frozen by Birds Eye from the early 1960s and quickly became a pub-menu staple, usually served in a small wicker basket with chips and a pot of tartare sauce. Real scampi is made from langoustines, which are abundant in Scottish and Irish waters. The majority of frozen pub scampi uses whole langoustine tails; lower-end products use formed scampi pieces from broken tails.
